newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration debating air quality rule.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration debating air quality rule.

text.p: The Clinton administration is still debating whether to set stricter air quality standards, but expects to have a tentative plan within two weeks, an administration official said on Monday.
"We are still at the point of constructive discussion. We believe these are valuable, necessary discussions that are still at a very constructive stage," the official said.

Several environmental sources said they understood that talks between the Environmental Protection Agency and other agencies, being overseen by the White House, were deadlocked and near the point at which Vice President Al Gore or even President Bill Clinton would have to step in to make a decision.
But the administration official said: "We have not crossed that bridge yet" on needing Gore or Clinton to intervene.

Sources in industry and environmental groups characterised the talks as EPA Administrator Carol Browner, with backing from the White House Council on Environmental Quality, defending her proposal to tighten standards on smog and soot against other departments and White House officials who argue the new rules would have harsh economic effects.

Industry groups have said the tighter standards could cost billions of dollars in pollution controls to meet, but environmentalists and health advocates said they would prolong thousands of lives and improve public health.

Browner has said the Clean Air Act requires her to base the standard on public health protections without regard to economic effects. Those are considered later when the administration plans how to meet the standards, she has said.

Because of the early involvement of the White House National Economic Council, the Office of Management and Budget and the Council on Environmental Quality, the plan the EPA submits later this month is expected to reflect the administration's view, although it still could be changed before the rule is finalised in July.

"Sometime within the next two weeks a package will go over that hopefully will be honed fairly significantly, but some discussions will continue between OMB and the EPA," the administration official said.
With the White House decision expected shortly, letters continued to circulate in Congress for and against the EPA proposal.
Nine members of the Senate Agriculture Committee, including two Democrats, wrote Browner saying they were concerned stricter standards would cut farmers' profits.
Thomas Harkin of Iowa and Robert Kerrey of Nebraska were Democrats that signed the letter spearheaded by Committee Chairman Richard Lugar, an Indiana Republican.
Meanwhile Jim Jeffords of Vermont was the only Senate Republican so far who signed a letter supporting the stronger standards.
Letters also are circulating in the House, with many Republicans and a number of midwestern and southern Democrats opposed to the EPA proposal.
